DBGWroAot-4.title: The Harem Conspiracy That Killed Ramesses III
DBGWroAot-4.description:
Three thousand years ago, an Egyptian court sentenced more than thirty people for a plot against their pharaoh. The record of their trial survives, and it never says what happened to the king.

This is the story of the harem conspiracy against Ramesses the Third. One of his wives, Tiye, wanted the throne for her son Pentawer, though it had been promised to another son. She found allies close to the king, from the chief of his chamber to a commander of the army, and the plotters even had wax figures made with a magic roll that belonged to Ramesses himself. What followed was a trial in which the accused lost even their names, and the court itself ended up on trial.

For more than a century, historians argued over whether the king had been murdered at all. Then, in 2012, researchers looked under the linen collar around his neck, while a young man in a coffin with no name, found in the same hidden tomb, raised a question that is still open.

JQyt0JaRJ8Q.title: Hephaestus, Aphrodite & Ares: The Net That Caught the God of War (Greek Gods, Part 4)
JQyt0JaRJ8Q.description:
Hera threw her own son off Olympus because he was born lame. A later tradition says he answered with a golden throne that trapped her the moment she sat down.

In this part of our Greek Gods series, Hephaestus grows up in a sea cave, becomes the craftsman Olympus cannot do without, and marries Aphrodite. But Aphrodite loves Ares, the god of war, and Homer's Odyssey tells what happened when the Sun saw them together: Hephaestus forged chains too fine for any god to see.

The net falls, the gods crowd in to look, and one of them says he would gladly take the chains himself. Only Poseidon does not laugh. Hesiod gives Aphrodite and Ares three children: Fear, Panic, and Harmony.

MZ5I5s2hapA.title: The God Who Sacrificed His Hand to Save the World — Norse Mythology Tale about Trust and Sacrifice
MZ5I5s2hapA.description:
In Norse mythology, one god was willing to put his hand inside the mouth of the most dangerous wolf in the gods' world. But Tyr knew there was only one way to prove that Fenrir could be trusted.

As the gods sought to bind the growing wolf, they turned to Gleipnir — a magical binding forged by the dwarfs. Fenrir agreed to test it, but only if one of the gods placed a hand in his jaws as a guarantee.

Tyr accepted.

What followed became one of the most famous and tragic moments in Norse mythology — the sacrifice that cost Tyr his hand and left Fenrir bound.

Mrai30wItZI.title: How Humans Learned to Cross Entire Oceans Without a Compass #history #animation #story #geography
Mrai30wItZI.description:
How do you cross thousands of kilometers of open ocean when you have no compass and no land in sight? For centuries, Polynesian wayfinders found their way across the Pacific by learning to read signals hidden in the natural world.

Stars, winds, ocean swells, clouds, currents and even birds could reveal what was happening beyond the horizon. This knowledge was memorized and passed from navigator to navigator, allowing skilled wayfinders to navigate enormous stretches of ocean without modern instruments.

In 1976, the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti using traditional non-instrument navigation, with Mau Piailug serving as navigator. The voyage helped demonstrate the remarkable knowledge behind traditional Pacific wayfinding.

NHMGOOVNNk0.title: A Kingdom Refused to Sell Its Horses. So China Sent an Army
NHMGOOVNNk0.description:
Emperor Wu of Han offered a thousand pieces of gold and a horse made of gold for the best horses of a kingdom far to the west. Its nobles refused. They had done the arithmetic, and they were sure China could never send an army that far.

In the second century BCE, the most dangerous enemy of the Han dynasty was the Xiongnu, nomads of the northern steppe who lived on horseback, and to catch them the emperor needed better horses than his own. More than two thousand miles away, in the Ferghana Valley, the kingdom of Dayuan had horses that, people said, sweated blood and were descended from horses of heaven. The envoy sent to buy them lost his temper, smashed the golden horse, and was ambushed and killed at Dayuan's border. So began the War of the Heavenly Horses.

When the first army limped back to the frontier with one or two men in ten, the emperor shut the Jade Gate against his own soldiers. Then he sent sixty thousand more, with a hundred thousand oxen and two experts in judging horses, and at a capital with no wells, the Han moved the river. The court historian Sima Qian was blunt about what it all cost, and about who was to blame.

_1h_EAjb_wk.title: The Gallic Sack of Rome after the Battle of the Allia in 390 BC
_1h_EAjb_wk.description:
Rome would one day become the center of one of history's greatest empires. But in 390 BCE, its future came terrifyingly close to ending.

A Gallic army under Brennus defeated the Romans at the Allia River and marched into Rome. With the Roman army broken, the city's defenders were forced back to the Capitoline Hill — the last stronghold they still held.

For one night, the fate of Rome rested on a handful of defenders, a desperate position, and an alarm that came just in time. The Romans survived, but the disaster left a deep mark on Roman memory.

This is the story of the night Rome was sacked, the Capitoline Hill became its final refuge, and a city that would eventually shape the ancient world came frighteningly close to disappearing.

_eKElXW9Hk4.title: Divers Found a 2,000-Year-Old Greek Computer in a Shipwreck
_eKElXW9Hk4.description:
In 1900, a boat of Greek sponge divers sheltering from a storm found an ancient shipwreck off the island of Antikythera. Among the statues they raised was a shapeless lump of corroded bronze that nobody paid much attention to.

Two years later the lump split apart, and archaeologist Valerios Stais saw something that did not seem to belong in the ancient world: a gear wheel. Then another, and another, packed inside a case the size of a shoebox. For decades the Antikythera mechanism stayed a puzzle, until X-ray scans in 2005 revealed about thirty surviving gears and thousands of tiny letters hidden beneath the corrosion.

Turn its handle and the machine moved the sky. It tracked the Sun and the Moon through the zodiac, predicted eclipses years in advance, kept track of the Olympic Games, and even copied the uneven speed of the real Moon. So how was something this intricate built in ancient Greece, and why is it the only one we have?

aE1EFPZLo3E.title: Zeus, Poseidon and Hades Drew Lots for the Universe (Greek Gods, Part 1)
aE1EFPZLo3E.description:
Three brothers shook three lots in a helmet, and whatever each of them drew, he would rule forever. This is how Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades divided the universe of Greek mythology, and why the brother who drew the worst became the god the Greeks mostly avoided naming.

It begins with their father. Cronus had been told that one of his children would overthrow him, so every time Rhea gave birth, he swallowed the child. When the sixth was coming, she hid in a cave on Crete and handed him a stone wrapped in a baby's blanket instead. That child was Zeus. He came back, forced his father to bring up his brothers and sisters, and what followed was a ten-year war against the Titans that neither side could finish.

The winners had a universe and no agreement about who owned it. According to Homer, they did not fight over it. They drew lots. But Poseidon never accepted the result; one part of the world was left out of the draw on purpose, and the brother who got the dead ended up with a very different name: Plouton, the rich one.

This is Part 1 of our Greek Gods series. Next: their three sisters, swallowed by the same father, freed by the same brother, and given no kingdom at all. Subscribe to Animated Tales for more animated stories from mythology, legends, history, and the ancient world.

asH-WNx94kA.title: Marriage, Harvest or Hearth: Which Goddess Held the Real Power? (Greek Gods, Part 2)
asH-WNx94kA.description:
Three brothers drew lots for the universe. Their three sisters were never given one, and yet one of them stopped the grain for a whole year until the king of the sky gave in.

Hera, Demeter and Hestia were swallowed by their father Cronus and brought back up by Zeus, just like their brothers. But when Zeus, Poseidon and Hades divided the sky, the sea and the dead, the sisters got no kingdom. In Greek mythology, they got something smaller and closer to home: a marriage, a harvest, and a fire in the middle of the house.

Hera became queen of the gods, married to the least faithful husband in Greek myth, and still her temple at Olympia stood for more than a century before his. Demeter, whose daughter Persephone was carried down to the land of the dead, found a way to fight back without a kingdom of her own. And Hestia, asked in marriage by Poseidon and Apollo, swore never to marry at all.

This is Part 2 of our Greek Gods series. Next: three gods who were never supposed to be born, one of them straight out of her father's head. Subscribe to Animated Tales for more animated stories from mythology, legends, history, and the ancient world.

e5QGFphahok.title: From a Gilded Heir on a Raft to a Lost City on European Maps: The Story of El Dorado
e5QGFphahok.description:
El Dorado was not a city. It was a man covered in gold dust, standing on a raft in the middle of a mountain lake, and the Spaniards who came hunting for him never saw it.

This is the legend of El Dorado as the chronicler Juan Rodríguez Freyle wrote it down in 1636. An heir of the Muisca spent six years fasting in a cave, was dusted with powdered gold, and from a reed raft in Lake Guatavita, Colombia, threw gold into the water while the shore roared. The Spaniards heard of it in Quito. Then the name left the man and became a place, a city and a lake called Parime on European maps for two hundred years. Walter Raleigh sailed after it twice.

A gold raft found in a cave at Pasca in 1969 may or may not show that lake, and whether the ceremony happened as Freyle tells it, nobody can prove. Freyle himself went hunting for gold at another sacred lake, and he confesses it.

hsGI3xlJ-SY.title: The Last Lydian King — The Prophecy That Destroyed His Kingdom #history #oracle #prophecy #delfi
hsGI3xlJ-SY.description:
Croesus thought an oracle had promised him victory over Persia. Instead, his decision destroyed his own kingdom.

This is the story of the prophecy that was true — but not in the way Croesus expected.

Croesus, king of Lydia, had wealth, power, and one dangerous question:

Should he go to war with Persia?

Before attacking Cyrus the Great, Croesus turned to the famous oracle at Delphi. The answer seemed to promise exactly what he wanted to hear.

If Croesus crossed the Halys River and attacked Persia, the oracle said, a great empire would be destroyed.

Croesus assumed the prophecy meant Persia.

He was wrong.

He crossed the river, fought Cyrus at Pteria, retreated to Sardis, and expected time to prepare for the next battle. Instead, Cyrus followed him.

Fourteen days later, Sardis fell.

Croesus was captured, and Lydia was destroyed.

Only then did the prophecy become clear.

The oracle had never said which empire would fall.

It had been Croesus' own assumption that doomed him.

This is the story of Croesus, the incredibly wealthy king who believed he had discovered the fate of Persia — only to discover that the prophecy had been about him all along.

nUQkW9Umv8M.title: The Battle of Marathon - The Battle Won by a Dead Man’s Army #history #ancient #greece #persian
nUQkW9Umv8M.description:
What if the warriors who died on a battlefield were said to keep fighting long after the battle was over?

In 490 BC, a Persian army landed at Marathon with Athens as its target. Outnumbered and divided over whether to attack, the Athenians ultimately chose to fight — and then did something the Persians never expected: they ran toward them.

The battle became a brutal clash of shields, spears and close combat before the Athenian wings turned inward and trapped the Persian center. Even after victory, the Athenians had to race back to Athens to stop the Persian fleet from reaching the city.

But the strangest part of the story came centuries later.

According to ancient traditions, Marathon was not truly silent after dark. People claimed they could still hear horses and men fighting on the battlefield — as if the warriors who died there had never stopped fighting. Other stories told of mysterious warriors and unexplained encounters surrounding the battle.

We cannot know whether the legends were true. But Marathon became more than a battlefield: a place where, according to legend, the living won the battle... and the dead never stopped fighting.

nxcTrVYjtcg.title: Hunahpu and Xbalanque Went Down to the Maya Underworld, Where Their Father Died
nxcTrVYjtcg.description:
The lords of the Maya underworld invited two brothers to a ball game. It was a trap, and the brothers knew it, because it was how their father had died.

This is the story of Hunahpu and Xbalanque, the hero twins of the Popol Vuh, the book of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala. It was written down in the 1550s, after the Spanish conquest, and copied by a priest around 1701. The twins go down to Xibalba, the underworld, and face the same lords who killed their father, Hun Hunahpu. They cross rivers of blood on their blowguns, greet every lord by name, spend the nights in the House of Darkness, the House of Cold and the House of Bats, and win the ball game with a rabbit, a turtle and two canes growing in their grandmother's house. The lords of death, it turns out, could not resist a good show.

No one knows how old the story is. Maya vases from a thousand years before the book show figures that may be the twins, but the book itself was written after the conquest, and scholars still argue about what it kept.

ovdOrU00qX4.title: The Ancient Ritual of Crowning Another Man to Die in the King's Place
ovdOrU00qX4.description:
When the moon went dark over ancient Assyria, the king's scholars had a way to save his life. They put another man on his throne, and when the danger had passed, they let that man die in the king's place.

In the seventh century BCE, Assyria was ruled by Esarhaddon, and hundreds of letters from his scholars survive to show how the substitute king ritual was done. A stand-in was washed, anointed and dressed in the king's robes, with a young woman beside him as his queen. The omens were recited before the sun god Shamash, and the real king stayed hidden in his palace while his scholars wrote to him as "the farmer".

In 671 BCE the substitute was someone who mattered: Damqi, the son of a high temple official in the Babylonian city of Akkad, who had been told by a prophetess that he would take over the kingship. The ritual itself was far older than Esarhaddon. Its earliest story comes from a Babylonian chronicle set more than a thousand years earlier in the city of Isin, and it ends the other way round, though historians suspect that tale is a legend.

tCUBTJ4WTFU.title: The Greek Gods Born Against All Odds - Athena, Apollo & Artemis (Greek Gods, Part 3)
tCUBTJ4WTFU.description:
Zeus heard the same prophecy that had haunted his father Cronus: his wife would bear a son who would be king of gods and men. So he did not wait. He swallowed her whole, and the daughter she was carrying came out of his own head.

In this part of our Greek Gods series, three gods who were never supposed to be born arrive anyway. Athena leaps out fully armed, wins Athens from her uncle Poseidon with an olive tree, and becomes her father's favourite. Leto, pregnant with Zeus's twins, is hunted across the earth by Hera until Delos, a bare rock that some tellings say floated loose on the sea, agrees to take her in.

Nine days of labour, a golden necklace nine cubits long, and a newborn god who speaks the moment he arrives. Apollo claims the lyre, the bow and the will of Zeus, and his twin sister Artemis grows up a hunter in the wild. One child never comes at all.

This is Part 3 of our Greek Gods series. Next: the god his mother threw off Olympus marries the most beautiful goddess, and catches her in a net. Subscribe to Animated Tales for more animated stories from mythology, legends, history and the ancient world.
